\begin{bankq}[id=SII18-P1-PHY-S2-Q09, source={Score-II - Test 18 (13 Feb 2024)}, paper=1, qno=9, type=multi, subtopic={Pendulums}, answer={A,B}, answer_src=key, difficulty=8, diff_parts={K3 S1 I2 C2 F1}, diff_note={concepts: standard problem in this chapter, pendulums, apply the relevant results | steps: apply the relevant results; compute}]
A (suitably made) wire coat hanger can perform small amplitude oscillation in the plane of the figure around the equilibrium positions shown. In positions (a) and (b) the long side is horizontal. The other two sides have equal length. The period of oscillation is the same in all cases.

\begin{center}
\bfigi{233.8}{SII18_p1phy_q9_hanger.png}
\end{center}

The figure does not contain any information beyond the dimensions given. Nothing is known, e.g., concerning the detailed distribution of mass.

\begin{qoptions}
\opt{A}{Center of mass must be somewhere on AD line [D is mid point of BC]}
\opt{B}{Time period of oscillation will be $2\pi\sqrt{\dfrac{\left(\frac{d_1^2}{4}+\frac{d_2^2}{4}\right)^{1/2}+\frac{d_2}{2}}{g}}$ \{Here BC = d$_1$, AD = d$_2$\}}
\opt{C}{Time period of oscillation will be $2\pi\sqrt{\dfrac{\left(\frac{d_1^2}{4}+\frac{d_2^2}{4}\right)^{1/2}+\frac{d_2}{4}}{g}}$ \{Here BC = d$_1$, AD = d$_2$\}}
\opt{D}{Center of mass of hanger can not be on line AD}
\end{qoptions}
\end{bankq}

 & & (T) & decreases and increases in a periodic manner \\

\end{tabular}

Phase space diagrams are useful tools in analyzing all kinds of dynamical problems. They are especially useful in studying the changes in motion as initial position and momentum are changed. Here we consider some simple dynamical systems for which phase space is a plane in which position is plotted along horizontal axis and momentum is plotted along vertical axis. The phase space diagram is x(t) vs. p(t) curve in this plane. The arrow on the curve indicates the time flow. For example, the phase space diagram for a particle moving with constant velocity is a straight line as shown in the figure. Similarly we may also plot momentum of a pendulum versus $\theta$ (with sign convention shown in figure (b)).\par
\bfig{78.7}{SA06_p2_phy_s2_q10_1.png}
